newsitem.title: CANADA: NHL-SALMING, THREE OTHERS INDUCTEES FOR HOCKEY HALL OF FAME.
newsitem.headline: NHL-SALMING, THREE OTHERS INDUCTEES FOR HOCKEY HALL OF FAME.

text.p: Swedish-born Borje Salming, an outstanding two-way defenceman who paved the way for other Europeans to join the National Hockey League, was one of four inductees announced Monday by the Hockey Hall of Fame.

Also to be inducted on Nov. 25 in Toronto are Al Arbour, who coached the New York Islanders during their four consecutive titles in the 1980s, Bobby Bauer, who played 10 years for the Boston Bruins in the 1930s and 1940s, and Bob Cole, who does play-by-play for "Hockey Night In Canada."

Salming will be inducted in the players' category, Bauer in the veteran players' category and Arbour in the builders' category. Cole will get the Foster Hewitt Memorial Award for excellence in hockey broadcasting.
Salming signed with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 1973 and in a six-year stretch was named as a first-team All-Star once and a second-teamer five times.
Salming played 17 seasons, collecting 150 goals and 737 assists. He twice was runner-up for the James Norris Trophy as the NHL's top defenceman.

Arbour and Scotty Bowman of the Detroit Red Wings are the only men to coach over 1,600 NHL games. Arbour won 781 games, most of them coming during his first stint with the Islanders. The Islanders are one of just three franchises to win four successive Stanley Cups, doing so from 1980 to 1983.
Arbour also played 14 seasons as a defenceman, winning Stanley Cup championships in 1954 with Detroit, 1961 with Chicago and 1962 and 1964 with Toronto.
He began his coaching career with the St. Louis Blues in 1970 and received the Lester Patrick Award in 1992 for contributions to the development of hockey in the United States.
Bauer, a right winger, had 20 goals as a rookie in the 1937-38 season. In 1940, he won the first of three Lady Byng Trophies as the league's most gentlemanly player.
He was a second-team All-Star four times and helped the Bruins win two Stanley Cups. He scored the winning goal against Detroit in the 1941 Finals.
Cole, who began his broadcasting career in 1956, replaced Bill Hewitt on "Hockey Night In Canada" on a full-time basis in the late 1970s.
